item.title: Discovery Before Solutions
item.author: gdevika423@gmail.com (Devika Jallegowda)
item.description:
Many product efforts fail because teams jump to solutions before fully understanding the underlying problem.

The tendency to solution quickly

Engineering teams are naturally inclined to build solutions. However, without careful discovery, teams risk solving the wrong problem.

Why discovery matters

Product discovery helps teams understand:

  • user workflows
  • operational constraints
  • existing system limitations

Example from enterprise operations

In many SAP environments, engineers perform repetitive monitoring checks. At first glance, the solution appears to be automation scripts.

However, the deeper issue is often a lack of centralized operational visibility.

Takeaway

Effective product development begins with understanding the problem space before committing to a solution.

item.title: Products vs Services
item.author: gdevika423@gmail.com (Devika Jallegowda)
item.description:
Context

Many technology organizations provide operational services before building products.

Observation

Services are typically customized for individual clients, while products aim to deliver repeatable solutions across many customers.

Example

Enterprise operations teams often perform manual tasks such as monitoring, incident response, or infrastructure maintenance.

Over time, recurring operational tasks may be automated and packaged into software systems.

This transformation represents a shift from service delivery to product design.

Takeaway

Product thinking often begins by identifying repeatable patterns within service workflows.

item.title: Thinking in Platforms
item.author: gdevika423@gmail.com (Devika Jallegowda)
item.description:
Context

Platforms emerge when systems are designed to support multiple users, workflows, and services.

Observation

Many internal tools begin as small utilities that solve specific problems for individual teams.

As these tools grow in capability, they often become shared platforms.

Example

Developer portals, CI systems, and internal automation frameworks frequently begin as small team tools before evolving into organization wide platforms.

Takeaway

Platform thinking requires designing systems that support extensibility, reuse, and multiple stakeholders.
